lesson.subtitle: Lesson 9 -- The Thing I Kept Working On
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Pedro Henrique Tadeu Alves da Silva | Lesson 9 -- The Thing I Kept Working On

listenings.text: Nobody warns you about the middle. Everybody talks about starting, and everybody talks about finishing, and the part that actually breaks people is the eleven days in between, when the thing is no longer new and it is not yet good. I have watched a lot of people in that stretch, and the ones who come out the other side are not the stubborn ones. That surprised me. The stubborn ones keep pushing on exactly the same idea for a week and end up with a slightly better version of something that was never going to work. The ones who survive do something different: they park it. They stop working on the difficult part and they finish something small and boring instead, on purpose. Then they come back two days later and the problem has usually changed shape. And the second thing they do is decide, out loud, how much longer they are willing to spend on it. Not because the number is right. Because having a number stops you from second-guessing yourself every four hours.

I spent nine hours once on two seconds of audio. A transition between a verse and a chorus, and it was not even wrong, it was just not beautiful, and I refused to leave it. I kept trying different versions, I avoided going to bed, and somewhere around hour seven I stopped being a producer and became a person defending a decision. The mix went out the next week. Nobody mentioned the transition. Nobody has ever mentioned it, and that is not because it is perfect, it is because two seconds in the middle of a song is two seconds. What I learned, very late, is that the feeling of being close is not information. It feels identical whether you are twenty minutes from finishing or four hours from realising it is a dead end. So now I do the boring thing. I decide in advance how long I am willing to spend, I write the number on a piece of paper, and when I get there I either call it or I ask somebody else to listen. Usually they say it is fine. Usually they are right.

extra_audio.text: Pedro says he decided to keep working on the transition for one more hour. He explains that he kept trying different versions and avoided asking anybody for help. He admits that he ended up in a rabbit hole and lost the momentum of the whole session. He says he finally agreed to park it and to finish something small instead. He adds that he came back two days later and managed to fix it in ten minutes. Then he asks the other person how they decide when to call it.
